nameStory: The willet gets its name from its loud, distinctive call that sounds like "will-will-willet" echoing across coastal marshes and beaches. This piercing cry is often the first thing that alerts birdwatchers to the presence of these robust shorebirds, making the name perfectly descriptive of their most notable behavior.
description: The willet is a large, sturdy shorebird that's the heavyweight champion of the sandpiper family's "shank" group. At first glance, it appears rather plain with mottled gray-brown plumage, but when it takes flight, it reveals dramatic black-and-white striped wings that flash like semaphores. These robust birds stand tall on long, sturdy legs and sport a straight, thick bill perfect for probing mudflats and shallow waters. They're noticeably larger and bulkier than most other sandpipers you'll encounter along New England's coast.

idTips.label: Wing pattern in flight
idTips.description: The most spectacular field mark - bold black and white stripes on the wings that create a striking contrast pattern visible from great distances when the bird is flying

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Noticeably large and robust for a sandpiper, with a thick neck and sturdy appearance that makes it look almost chunky compared to more delicate shorebirds

idTips.label: Bill characteristics
idTips.description: Straight, thick, dark bill that's substantial and blunt-tipped, perfect for probing into soft mud and sand with determined jabs

idTips.label: Leg color
idTips.description: Long, sturdy legs that are typically bluish-gray to dark gray, lacking the bright yellow of yellowlegs species

idTips.label: Voice
idTips.description: Loud, ringing "will-will-willet" call that carries far across open water and marshes, often given repeatedly when alarmed or territorial

idTips.label: Resting posture
idTips.description: When not feeding, often stands motionless with upright, alert posture on mudflats or at water's edge, appearing confident and territorial

habitat: Look for willets along New England's salt marshes, mudflats, beaches, and shallow coastal waters from spring through fall. They prefer areas where retreating tides expose rich feeding grounds of soft mud and sand, often alongside other shorebirds but maintaining their own space. During migration, they can also turn up at inland ponds and lakes, though coastal habitats remain their preferred territory.

seasonality.spring: Arrive in late April to May as migrants, with some individuals showing the beginning of breeding plumage patterns. Peak migration activity occurs in May when flocks can be found at prime feeding sites.
seasonality.summer: Present but less common, with most birds having moved north to breeding grounds. Those remaining show full breeding plumage with intricate neck patterning and are often more vocal and territorial.
seasonality.fall: Most abundant from July through September during fall migration, when adults and juveniles move through in waves. Young birds appear duller and less patterned than adults.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England, having departed for warmer southern coastal areas and Central America where they spend the cold months.

funFact: Despite looking rather drab when standing around, willets are the fighter jets of the shorebird world - they can reach speeds of over 50 mph in flight and are known to chase away birds many times their size, including herons and hawks, from their feeding territories with fearless aerial attacks.
confusionNotes: When not in flight, willets can be confused with godwits or other large sandpipers, but remember: willets have straight (not curved) bills and gray (not yellow) legs. The easiest memory trick is "willet wings wow" - wait to see those spectacular striped wings in flight for a positive ID, as no other New England shorebird has this dramatic pattern.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name "semipalmata" means "half-webbed," referring to the partial webbing between their toes that helps them walk on soft mud without sinking. This adaptation makes them excellent mudflat foragers but is only visible if you get an unusually close look at their feet.
compareHints: Among its Tringa relatives, the willet dwarfs both greater and lesser yellowlegs with its robust build and lacks their bright yellow legs entirely. While yellowlegs are elegant and slender, willets are the sturdy, no-nonsense members of the group. The willet's dramatic wing pattern in flight is completely unique among the shanks - yellowlegs show much more subtle wing markings and appear graceful rather than bold.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Tringa relatives, Greater Yellowlegs is larger than Lesser Yellowlegs and Solitary Sandpiper, with brighter yellow legs than either.
Compared to its Tringa cousins, the Solitary Sandpiper is smaller than both Greater and Lesser Yellowlegs with much darker, greenish legs instead of bright yellow ones.
Compared to its close relative the Greater Yellowlegs, the Lesser is noticeably smaller with a shorter, always-straight bill.
Wood Sandpiper is much smaller and more delicate than both Greater and Lesser Yellowlegs, with proportionally shorter legs and bill.
Compared to its New England relatives in the same genus, the Common Redshank is smaller than Greater Yellowlegs but similar in size to Lesser Yellowlegs, though much stockier in build.
Compared to its New England cousins, the spotted redshank has the brightest colored legs - much more vivid red-orange than the yellow of both yellowlegs species.
